speaker: Dana
text: First, a quick note on what this is. Insurance Daily is an AI-generated briefing. Every weekday morning we scan the industry trade press, pick out the stories that matter most to agents and brokers, and turn them into this show. The voices you are hearing are synthetic, and the script is written by AI from published reporting. We name our sources as we go so you can check them. But AI can and does get things wrong, so please treat this as a starting point and not as a source of record. Verify the detail before you act on anything you hear here.

speaker: Ray
text: Cyber just took the top spot again, and this time AI is the reason why. Travelers' latest Risk Index is out, reported by Claims Journal, and fifty eight percent of businesses now name cyber as their top concern, ahead of everything else on the list.

speaker: Dana
text: And the driver isn't just ransomware like it used to be. It's the speed AI is moving at with basically no governance around it. Businesses are adopting these tools faster than anyone's writing policy for them, internally or on the risk management side.

speaker: Ray
text: Which is exactly the gap an agent needs to be pointing at. If your commercial client is plugging AI into claims processing, customer service, underwriting, whatever it is, and their cyber policy was written two years ago, that conversation needs to happen now, not at renewal.

speaker: Dana
text: It's also just a great door-opener. Cyber's been a tough sell for some smaller commercial accounts. This gives you a stat straight from a major carrier's own research to start that appetite conversation.

speaker: Ray
text: Worth checking with your carriers too, on how they're actually underwriting AI exposure right now. That's evolving fast.

speaker: Dana
text: Alright. This is Insurance Daily, Thursday the twenty fourth of September. Coming up, we've got more on the property market and a look at what's moving in personal lines.

speaker: Ray
text: Let's start with weather, because there's actual live cat exposure on the board today. Insurance Journal is reporting a hurricane watch has been posted for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Nolo strengthens south of the island chain.

speaker: Dana
text: Nolo's still out there, winds around forty miles an hour, sitting about five hundred miles south of Honolulu last check. So it's not imminent, but it's moving.

speaker: Ray
text: If you've got any island business, homeowners, condo associations, commercial property on the Big Island, this is your call-your-clients moment. Remind them to document, secure loose property, and check flood status too, since wind and water don't always come from the same peril.

speaker: Dana
text: And late September, moving into a Pacific system, it's a reminder the season's not done anywhere. Keep an eye on binding restrictions if this thing organizes further.

speaker: Ray
text: Shifting to mitigation. Insurance Journal also has Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry announcing another twenty million dollars into the state's Fortified homes program. That brings total investment in Fortified projects this year alone to one hundred million dollars.

speaker: Dana
text: That's real money, and it's on top of what's already been a multi-year push. For agents in Louisiana, and honestly anywhere near the Gulf, Fortified roofs are becoming the go-to lever for both premium credits and just plain insurability in a tough coastal market.

speaker: Ray
text: Some of that twenty million is federal dollars flowing through, worth watching how the state structures applications so you can point clients toward it before the funding's spoken for.

speaker: Dana
text: Good conversation to have with any Louisiana homeowner who's staring at a renewal increase. Fortified isn't free, but state money narrows the gap.

speaker: Ray
text: North of the border now. Artemis is citing CatIQ data showing summer storms across the Canadian Prairies caused more than one point eight billion dollars in insured losses. Ten separate extreme weather events this summer alone.

speaker: Dana
text: The Insurance Bureau of Canada is now pushing governments for action on reducing that exposure. This isn't your book directly if you're U.S.-only, but it matters.

speaker: Ray
text: Right, because Canadian secondary-peril losses feed straight into global reinsurance treaty pricing. When cedents up north are absorbing numbers like that, it shows up in renewal terms for U.S. carriers too, especially on property cat treaties.

speaker: Dana
text: So if your carriers start tightening on convective storm and hail exposure at treaty renewal time, this is part of why. It's not just Texas and the Midwest driving that conversation anymore.

speaker: Ray
text: Trucking and commercial auto folks, pay attention here. Carrier Management reports the Department of Transportation has issued a ninety-day waiver on hours-of-service rules for drivers hauling gasoline and diesel. Took effect September sixteenth.

speaker: Dana
text: So instead of the usual fourteen-hour window, fuel haulers can now run up to sixteen hours in a twenty-four hour period. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is citing fuel supply and cost concerns.

speaker: Ray
text: For agents writing trucking risks, this changes the compliance picture your fuel-hauling clients are operating under, and it's worth flagging on the liability side. Longer hours behind the wheel, even temporarily, is the kind of thing that shows up in a fatigue-related claim down the line.

speaker: Dana
text: It's only ninety days on paper, but remind clients their E and O exposure doesn't pause just because DOT relaxed the rule. Document compliance with whatever the waiver actually requires.

speaker: Ray
text: Now, a distribution story that's worth watching closely. Insurance Journal reports Insurify has blocked Meta's personal AI agent, called Muse, from operating on its marketplace.

speaker: Dana
text: Insurify's the outfit that made news earlier this year partnering with OpenAI's ChatGPT, a move that actually moved the S and P insurance index at the time. Now they're drawing a line against a different AI player.

speaker: Ray
text: The details on exactly why are still thin, but the bigger picture is what matters for agents. Every major tech platform wants to be the front door for insurance shopping. Meta, OpenAI, Google, all of them experimenting with AI agents that could route consumers before they ever talk to a human.

speaker: Dana
text: So watch who's blocking whom. It tells you where the leads are actually flowing, and whether your agency's digital presence still shows up when a consumer's AI assistant goes looking for a quote.

speaker: Ray
text: Last one. Insurance Business America is reporting public adjusters have launched a new national conduct code for handling claims in the U.S. It's voluntary, aimed at bringing some consistency across the patchwork of state rules public adjusters operate under.

speaker: Dana
text: Voluntary is the key word there, no teeth yet. But if it gets traction, it could smooth out some of the friction agents see when a public adjuster gets involved on a client's claim, especially on the property side after a cat event.

speaker: Ray
text: Worth keeping half an eye on adoption. If it becomes something carriers and state associations actually recognize, it changes how you set expectations with clients who bring in a PA.

speaker: Dana
text: Alright, that's the rest of today's headlines.

speaker: Ray
text: Okay, one thing worth understanding today, and it's Florida again, but from a different angle. Artemis is reporting on a new note from Morningstar DBRS, the ratings agency, about the state of the Florida property market.

speaker: Dana
text: And their bottom line is basically this: the recovery is real, but it's rented, not owned. Morningstar DBRS says Florida's residential property market has recovered significantly over the past couple of years. Fewer insolvencies, new carriers coming in, some rate stability. But they're saying that recovery only holds up as long as reinsurance stays affordable and available.

speaker: Ray
text: So the message is: don't confuse a calmer market with a stable one. It's stable because the reinsurance towers held together at renewal. That's a very different thing.

speaker: Dana
text: Right. And for anyone who's forgotten how we got here, the whole Florida turnaround since twenty twenty three has been built on legislative reform, tort changes, and then carriers being able to actually buy reinsurance at a price that let them write business again. Take any one of those legs away and the stool wobbles.

speaker: Ray
text: Who does this help and hurt is the real question for us. If reinsurance capacity stays plentiful and pricing keeps softening at the June and July renewals next year, that flows straight through to admitted carriers' primary rates. That's good for retention on your Florida book.

speaker: Dana
text: But flip it. Any active hurricane season, any shock loss event, and reinsurers pull back or reprice hard. And Florida carriers, especially the newer, thinner-capitalized ones that grew fast during the recovery, don't have a lot of surplus cushion to absorb that themselves. They pass it straight to primary rate or they pull back appetite.

speaker: Ray
text: Which is exactly what agents lived through in twenty twenty two and twenty three. Non-renewals, MGAs pulling binding authority overnight, clients dumped into Citizens.

speaker: Dana
text: Morningstar DBRS isn't predicting that's about to happen again. They're just saying the whole structure is still dependent on that reinsurance layer being there and being affordable. It's a stability warning, not a crisis call.

speaker: Ray
text: So what does an agent actually do with this. You're not buying reinsurance, obviously. But it should change how much confidence you put in a Florida quote that looks unusually good right now.

speaker: Dana
text: Exactly. If a carrier's pricing has softened a lot, it's worth understanding whether that's because their reinsurance costs genuinely came down, or whether they're just under-pricing to grow market share ahead of a renewal that might not go their way. That's not something you can always see from the outside, but it's a fair question to ask a wholesaler or an MGA you're placing with.

speaker: Ray
text: And carrier financial strength ratings matter more here than in most states. If a carrier's rating gets flagged or downgraded because of reinsurance dependency, that's a real conversation with the client, particularly if there's a mortgage involved and lender requirements.

speaker: Dana
text: It's also a reason to keep a diversified panel of Florida markets rather than leaning hard on whoever's cheapest this quarter. If one carrier's whole story depends on reinsurance staying cheap, you don't want your entire book sitting with them.

speaker: Ray
text: Nothing to action today, but it's the kind of report worth filing away. Next hurricane season's renewal cycle is the real test of whether this holds.

speaker: Dana
text: Speaking of hurricane season, let's get back to what's actually happening in the Pacific right now.

speaker: Ray
text: Quick hits before we go. Artemis is reporting Liberty Mutual Investments has hired Paschal Brooks as Managing Director and Head of Insurance Solutions and Capital Markets. He's an ILS veteran, and this looks like Liberty Mutual leaning harder into capital markets alongside its traditional balance sheet.

speaker: Dana
text: Also from Artemis, Nascent Re, the Bermuda transformer vehicle, issued two more preferred share ILS deals, twenty million dollars each for accounts called Quinton and Stevenage. Third and fourth series out of that vehicle now. Just more evidence capacity keeps finding its way through these structures.

speaker: Ray
text: And Insurance Journal has AM Best revising its outlook to positive for Farmers Mutual Hail Insurance Company of Iowa, affirming that A minus rating. Good sign of stability for agents leaning on FMH for crop and hail business.

speaker: Dana
text: That's Insurance Daily for Thursday the twenty fourth of September. Back tomorrow morning with more.

speaker: Ray
text: See you then.
